title: Ezekiel 45:18–25
context: The Lord GOD gives a festival calendar. On the first day of the first month a young bull is offered to cleanse the sanctuary, with blood placed on the doorposts of the house, the corners of the altar ledge, and the gate of the inner court; the same is done on the seventh day for anyone who errs or is simple (compare Leviticus 4:27; Numbers 15:28). Passover is kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, with seven days of unleavened bread, and the prince provides a bull as a sin offering for himself and for all the people, followed by daily burnt offerings and a goat for a sin offering. The same provision is made at the feast in the seventh month, commonly identified with the feast of booths (compare Leviticus 23:34; Numbers 29:12). This calendar differs in several details from Numbers 28–29, and interpreters have long noted the differences without agreeing on how to explain them. That the prince offers for himself (45:22) is commonly noted in discussions of his identity (compare Hebrews 7:27). The question of sacrifices in this vision is treated at 40:38–49 and 44:15–31. Readers in both traditions take the temple vision of chapters 40–48 in the ways named at 40:1–16. Arminian and Reformed readers generally treat God’s provision for cleansing and his desire for ordered worship as shared ground.

verses.text: “ ‘The Lord GOD says: “In the first month, on the first day of the month, you shall take a young bull without defect, and you shall cleanse the sanctuary.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a young bull offered on the first day of the first month to cleanse the sanctuary. The year begins with purification.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s concern that his dwelling be kept holy. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse within the vision, holding the sacrifice question in light of Hebrews 10 with care.

verses.text: The priest shall take of the blood of the sin offering and put it on the door posts of the house, and on the four corners of the ledge of the altar, and on the posts of the gate of the inner court.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priest putting the blood of the sin offering on the doorposts, altar ledge, and inner gate. The whole sanctuary is cleansed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an echo of the law’s cleansing rites (compare Leviticus 8:15). Both traditions commonly read the verse within the vision, without pressing beyond its setting.

verses.text: So you shall do on the seventh day of the month for everyone who errs, and for him who is simple. So you shall make atonement for the house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the same done on the seventh day for anyone who errs or is simple. God provides for unintentional sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see provision for those who sin in ignorance (compare Numbers 15:28). Readers in both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about God’s care for the weak and mistaken.

verses.text: “ ‘ “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, you shall have the Passover, a feast of seven days; unleavened bread shall be eaten.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Passover kept on the fourteenth day of the first month with seven days of unleavened bread. Deliverance is remembered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Passover continued in the vision (compare Exodus 12:18; Numbers 28:16–17). Both traditions commonly read the verse as celebrating God’s saving acts.

verses.text: On that day the prince shall prepare for himself and for all the people of the land a bull for a sin offering.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the prince preparing a sin offering for himself and for all the people. That he offers for himself is commonly noted when asking who he is.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same detail and compare Hebrews 7:27, where Christ needs no offering for himself. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the prince’s identity with care.

verses.text: The seven days of the feast he shall prepare a burnt offering to the LORD, seven bulls and seven rams without defect daily the seven days; and a male goat daily for a sin offering.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see daily burnt offerings and a daily goat for a sin offering during the seven days. Worship is abundant and regular.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see generous provision for the feast. Both traditions commonly read the verse within the vision, holding the sacrifice question in light of Hebrews 10:12 and 10:18 with care.

verses.text: He shall prepare a meal offering, an ephah for a bull, an ephah for a ram, and a hin of oil to an ephah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see meal offerings and oil given with each bull and ram. The offerings are complete, generous, and carefully set.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the detailed provision for worship. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the vision’s festival calendar of generous worship.

verses.text: “ ‘ “In the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month, during the feast, he shall do like that for seven days. He shall make the same provision for sin offering, the burnt offering, the meal offering, and the oil.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the same provision made at the feast in the seventh month. The calendar is consistent across both halves of the year.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the feast commonly identified with booths (compare Leviticus 23:34). Both traditions commonly read the verse within a calendar that differs in details from Numbers 28–29.
